correctness.rationale: For each base edge, two precisely specified legal square-cycle hops composed with the universal vertical matching hop are exactly the two diagonal transpositions on its four-cycle; outside that square they cancel. Those transpositions generate independent symmetric groups on the connected components of the bipartite double cover D=G times K_2. A connected base has connected D iff it contains an odd cycle; otherwise D has two connected parts equal to the bipartition classes of G square K_2. In the bipartite case all hops necessarily exchange the classes, while the vertical hop does so, proving exact wreath product equality. The singleton case is included. The standalone verifier independently enumerated all 77,477 hops across 49 connected base graphs, checking group orders and square-switch supports. General quantifiers are proved symbolically, not extrapolated from enumeration.

originality.rationale: The motivating 13 October 2026 primary paper explicitly poses both the cycle-prism and hypercube leap-group problems (Question 5.4) and asks about graph products (Question 5.5), while its statements in Sections 2 and 5 do not cover the classification proved here. The four-cycle switch lemma produces edge transpositions of a double cover, distinguishing this theorem from results on hop existence, matching counts, and derangements inside a fixed permutation group. Dedicated searches for mathematical aliases and comparisons of related published mathematical statements found no equivalent or stronger result. value.rationale: The theorem simultaneously answers the explicitly stated 2026 open cycle-prism and hypercube leap-group problems, and resolves an entire natural Cartesian-product class with a sharp bipartiteness dichotomy. It establishes an underlying square-switch mechanism and a double-cover explanation, rather than merely recalculating small groups. For nonbipartite G, every vertex permutation of its prism is a leap; for bipartite G, every bipartition-preserving or swapping permutation is a leap. These exact reachability descriptions have direct structural and enumerative significance.
